l: Orestes’s vengeance, The Odyssey, BOOK III
s: Orestes’s vengeance consists of returning from Athens and killing Aegisthus, who murdered Agamemnon. His act is praised as a noble vengeance that will preserve his name through time.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK III
s: The suitors are numerous and hostile to Telemachus, ill-treating him, plotting his ruin, and consuming his property. Telemachus doubts that either the gods or Ulysses will return to drive them away.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Minerva directs Nestor and his household to complete their religious offerings, then departs in the form of an eagle. Nestor welcomes Telemachus into his house, arranges a sacrifice to Minerva, and sends Telemachus toward Lacedaemon with Pisistratus. After the sacrifice and a communal meal, Telemachus and Pisistratus travel by chariot from Pylos, spend the night at Pherae, and continue their journey.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Minerva tells Nestor to cut the tongues of the victims, prepare drink-offerings, and go to bed. She agrees that Telemachus should stay at Nestor’s house, but returns to the ship to encourage her crew and says she must go to the Cauconians. She later flies away in the form of an eagle, and comes to accept Nestor’s sacrifice.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Telemachus stays at Nestor’s house instead of sleeping on his ship. He takes part in the sacrifice to Minerva, is washed and clothed by Polycaste, and then leaves Pylos in a chariot with Pisistratus. He spends the night at Pherae and continues toward Lacedaemon.

l: Nestor, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Nestor persuades Minerva and Telemachus to stay at his house, recognizing Minerva in the eagle and praying for her favor. He organizes and participates in a sacrifice to Minerva, then provides Telemachus with horses, provisions, and Pisistratus as a traveling companion.

l: Pisistratus, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Pisistratus sleeps in the room over the gateway with Telemachus. He helps prepare the heifer for sacrifice, drives the chariot carrying Telemachus, and spends the night with him at Pherae before continuing the journey.

l: Telemachus's crew, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Minerva says that Telemachus’s crew consists of young men who have taken the voyage out of friendship. At Nestor’s request, they leave the ship and attend the sacrifice, while two men remain in charge of the vessel.

l: Pylos, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Pylos is the place from which Telemachus and Pisistratus depart by chariot. They leave its high citadel behind them as they travel toward Lacedaemon.

l: Nestor’s house, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Nestor’s house provides lodging for Telemachus, who sleeps there with Pisistratus. The household prepares the sacrifice, receives the guests for a meal, and supplies provisions for Telemachus’s journey.

l: the ship, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Minerva and Telemachus initially plan to return to the ship, but Nestor persuades Telemachus to stay at his house. Minerva returns to the ship to keep its young crew in good heart, and two men remain in charge while the crew attends the sacrifice.

l: chariot, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Nestor orders that Telemachus be sent to Lacedaemon in a chariot. Pisistratus drives the chariot, which carries Telemachus from Pylos to Pherae and onward through the open country.

l: horses, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Nestor provides his best and fleetest horses for Telemachus’s journey. They are yoked to the chariot and carry Telemachus and Pisistratus swiftly from Pylos toward Lacedaemon.

l: heifer, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Nestor has a broad-browed, year-old heifer brought from the plain for Minerva. Its horns are gilded, and it is killed, cut up, and offered during the sacrifice.

l: sacrifice to Minerva, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Nestor promises Minerva a gilded-horned heifer after she appears as an eagle. The sacrifice includes prayers, barley meal, burnt thigh bones wrapped in fat, wine offerings, and the roasting and eating of the remaining meat.

l: Telemachus's journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: Nestor sends Telemachus toward Lacedaemon with Pisistratus in a chariot. They leave Pylos, spend the night at Pherae with Diocles, and continue their journey after dawn.

l: religious ritual, The Odyssey, As he spoke the sun set and it came on dark, whereon Minerva said,
s: The ritual includes cutting the victims’ tongues, making drink-offerings, washing hands, sprinkling barley meal, praying, burning offerings, and sharing the cooked meat. Nestor performs these acts with his sons, household, Telemachus’s crew, and Minerva’s favor.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Telemachus and Pisistratus arrive in Lacedaemon and receive lavish hospitality at Menelaus’s palace during wedding celebrations. Menelaus and Helen recognize Telemachus as Odysseus’s son and recount Odysseus’s hardships, his disguised entry into Troy, and his bravery in the Trojan Horse. The company grieves for the dead and for Odysseus, who remains missing, until Helen drugs the wine to relieve their sorrow. Telemachus and Pisistratus then retire to sleep in the forecourt.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Telemachus travels with Pisistratus to Lacedaemon and is welcomed into Menelaus’s palace. Menelaus and Helen recognize him as the son of Odysseus, and he weeps when Odysseus is mentioned. He asks Menelaus to send them to bed after hearing the stories about Troy.

l: Pisistratus, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Pisistratus accompanies Telemachus to Lacedaemon as Nestor’s escort. He explains Telemachus’s difficult situation and urges Menelaus to end the weeping during supper, drawing on his own grief for his brother Antilochus.

l: Menelaus, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Menelaus welcomes Telemachus and Pisistratus, provides them with food, baths, clothing, and lodging, and recognizes Telemachus as Odysseus’s son. He recalls his long journey home, the deaths of his companions, and Odysseus’s courage and endurance at Troy.

l: Helen, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Helen recognizes Telemachus’s likeness to Odysseus and recounts how Odysseus entered Troy disguised as a wounded beggar. She drugs the wine with an Egyptian herb to dispel the company’s sorrow and later orders beds to be prepared for the guests.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Odysseus remains missing, causing grief to his father, Penelope, and Telemachus. Menelaus and Helen praise his endurance, intelligence, courage, and skill in gathering information at Troy and protecting the Greek warriors in the Trojan Horse.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: The heading states that the suitors in Ithaca plot against Telemachus while he is away, but the events of their plot are not narrated in this unit.

l: Lacedaemon, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Lacedaemon is the low-lying city to which Telemachus and Pisistratus travel. They arrive there and go directly to Menelaus’s palace.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Ithaca is described as Telemachus’s home, where he has been left without supporters because Odysseus is absent. Menelaus says he had hoped to bring Telemachus, his goods, his son, and all his people away from Ithaca.

l: Troy, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Troy is the enemy city where Odysseus gathered information while disguised and where the Greek warriors used the wooden horse. The losses and hardships suffered there remain a source of grief for Menelaus, Pisistratus, Helen, and Telemachus.

l: the voyage from Troy, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Menelaus says that it took him nearly eight years to return home after traveling through many lands. He contrasts his difficult return with Odysseus’s continued absence and uncertainty about whether Odysseus is alive.

l: the Trojan War, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: The war is remembered through the deaths of many Achaeans, the destruction and suffering connected with Troy, and the exploits of Odysseus and the other warriors. Menelaus, Helen, and Pisistratus mourn those who died.

l: Odysseus’s disguise in Troy, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Odysseus covered himself with wounds and bruises, dressed in rags, and entered Troy looking like a menial or beggar. Helen recognized him, questioned him, washed and anointed him, gave him clothes, and kept his mission secret until he returned safely to the Greek camp.

l: Trojan Horse, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Menelaus recalls hiding inside the wooden horse with the bravest Argives while waiting to attack the Trojans. When Helen circled the horse and imitated the voices of the warriors’ wives, Odysseus stopped Anticlus from answering and thereby saved them all.

l: Menelaus's house, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Menelaus’s palace is richly furnished with bronze, gold, amber, ivory, and silver. Telemachus and Pisistratus are bathed, clothed, fed, and given beds there while Menelaus and Helen receive them as honored guests.

l: Telemachus's journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Telemachus and Pisistratus travel to Lacedaemon in search of Menelaus’s counsel. They arrive during Menelaus’s wedding feast, speak with him and Helen about Odysseus, and spend the night at his palace.

l: hospitality and feast, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Menelaus’s household welcomes the travelers by caring for their horses, bathing and clothing them, and serving them an abundant meal. The palace hosts a feast with relatives and neighbors, a bard, and tumblers in honor of two weddings.

l: grief for the dead and missing, The Odyssey, BOOK IV
s: Menelaus grieves for those who died at Troy and especially for Odysseus, whose fate is unknown. Pisistratus remembers his dead brother Antilochus, while Telemachus, Helen, Menelaus, and Pisistratus all weep before Helen drugs the wine to ease their sorrow.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Menelaus tells Telemachus how Idothea helped him capture Proteus in Egypt and learn how to complete his sea voyage home. Proteus reveals that Ulysses is alive but held by Calypso, that Ajax drowned, and that Agamemnon was murdered by Aegisthus. Menelaus says that the gods will grant him a blessed afterlife and offers Telemachus gifts, but Telemachus declines the horses because Ithaca lacks suitable open ground. Menelaus agrees to give him a precious silver mixing bowl instead.

l: Menelaus, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Menelaus questions Telemachus in Lacedaemon and listens to his account of the suitors. He recounts his detention in Egypt, his capture of Proteus, and what he learned about the surviving and dead Achaeans. He offers Telemachus horses and a precious mixing bowl, agreeing to give him the bowl instead of the horses.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Telemachus tells Menelaus that he has come to learn what happened to his father and describes how the suitors are consuming his household and estate. He asks Menelaus not to soften the truth about Ulysses. He declines horses as a gift because Ithaca has little level ground, but accepts the offer of a piece of plate.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Ulysses is identified as Telemachus’s father and as a man who formerly served the Achaeans loyally against the Trojans. Proteus says that Ulysses is alive on an island, sorrowing in the house of Calypso, who keeps him prisoner and prevents his return because he has no ships or sailors.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: The suitors are consuming Telemachus’s estate, killing his sheep and oxen, and seeking his mother in marriage. Menelaus condemns them as cowards and says that Ulysses would soon deal with them if he returned.

l: the Achaeans, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: The Achaeans were harassed by the Trojans, and Menelaus asks Proteus what became of them after the war. Proteus says that many are dead, while many others remain alive, and identifies Ajax and Agamemnon among those who perished and Ulysses among those still unable to return.

l: immortal gods, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: The gods detain Menelaus in Egypt because his hecatombs have not fully satisfied them and later require him to offer sacrifices before completing his voyage. They are described as strict about receiving their dues. They also determine that Menelaus will live after death in the Elysian plain.

l: Idothea, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Idothea, daughter of Proteus, takes pity on Menelaus when he is stranded at Pharos. She tells him how to ambush and hold Proteus, provides seal skins for the ambush, digs the pits, and places ambrosia under the men’s noses to counter the seals’ smell.

l: Proteus, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Proteus is an old immortal Egyptian who lives under the sea and knows the sea and the events taking place in distant lands. Menelaus and three companions seize him while he sleeps among his seals, despite his transformations into various creatures, fire, water, and a tree. After being forced to resume his true form, Proteus tells Menelaus how to complete his voyage and reports the fates of the Achaeans.

l: Agamemnon, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Agamemnon survives the voyage from Troy and reaches his homeland, but Aegisthus lures him to a banquet and kills him afterward. Menelaus later raises a barrow to preserve Agamemnon’s memory.

l: Aegisthus, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Aegisthus prepares an ambush for Agamemnon after receiving word that he has arrived. He invites Agamemnon to a banquet and kills him when it is over, while all of Agamemnon’s followers and Aegisthus’s men are also killed.

l: Calypso, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Calypso keeps Ulysses prisoner in her house on an island. Her presence prevents Ulysses from returning home because he has no ships or sailors.

l: Lacedaemon, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Lacedaemon is the place to which Telemachus makes his long sea voyage in order to visit Menelaus and ask about Ulysses.

l: Egypt, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Menelaus is detained in Egypt after the gods refuse to let him continue until he has satisfied them with sacrifices. Proteus tells him to return to the heaven-fed stream of Egypt and offer holy hecatombs before completing his voyage.

l: Pharos, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Pharos is an island near Egypt with a good harbour from which ships can reach the open sea after taking in water. Menelaus is becalmed there for twenty days until Idothea helps him.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Ithaca is Telemachus’s homeland and the place to which Ulysses has not yet returned. Telemachus says that it has little level ground, no racecourses, and terrain better suited to goats than horses.

l: the voyage from Troy, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Menelaus’s voyage home is delayed first by the gods and then by a lack of wind near Pharos. After receiving instructions from Proteus, offering sacrifices in Egypt, and appeasing the gods, Menelaus makes a quick passage home with a fair wind. Ulysses’s voyage home remains unfinished because Calypso holds him on an island.

l: the Trojan War, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: The Trojan War is recalled as the conflict in which the Achaeans were harassed by the Trojans. Menelaus reminds Telemachus that Ulysses served the Achaeans loyally during that conflict.

l: the capture of Proteus, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Menelaus and three trusted men hide in pits beneath seal skins and wait for Proteus to finish counting his seals and fall asleep. They seize him, maintain their grip through his transformations, and force him to reveal the gods’ demands and the fates of the Achaeans.

l: the killing of Agamemnon, The Odyssey, When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Menelaus rose
s: Aegisthus arranges the murder of Agamemnon by inviting him to a banquet after his return home and attacking him when the feast is over. Agamemnon’s followers and Aegisthus’s men are killed as well, and Menelaus later raises a barrow in Agamemnon’s memory.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: The suitors learn that Telemachus has sailed from Ithaca to Pylos and Lacedaemon to seek news of Ulysses, so Antinous organizes an attempt to murder him on his return. Medon tells Penelope about the plot, while Euryclea admits that she helped Telemachus depart without Penelope’s knowledge. Penelope prays to Minerva, who sends her a reassuring dream promising that Telemachus will return, though the goddess does not reveal whether Ulysses is alive. The suitors sail to Asteris and wait in ambush between Ithaca and Samos.

l: the suitors, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: The suitors learn that Telemachus has gone to Pylos and Lacedaemon, and they become alarmed. They plot to murder him, prepare a ship with twenty men, and sail to Asteris to ambush him.

l: Antinous, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Antinous is one of the suitors’ ringleaders and becomes enraged when he learns that Telemachus has sailed away. He orders that a ship and twenty men be prepared so that he can lie in wait for Telemachus between Ithaca and Samos.

l: Telemachus, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Telemachus has secretly sailed from Ithaca to Pylos and Lacedaemon to seek news of his father. The suitors plan to murder him before he can return, but Minerva assures Penelope in a vision that he will come back.

l: Penelope, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Penelope learns from Medon that the suitors are plotting to kill Telemachus and is overcome with grief. She prays to Minerva for his safety, then receives a comforting dream in which Minerva assures her that Telemachus will return.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Ulysses is remembered as a just and generous man who treated people well. Penelope remains anxious about whether he is alive or dead, but the vision sent by Minerva refuses to say.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Minerva hears Penelope’s prayer and sends a vision in the likeness of Penelope’s sister Iphthime to comfort her. The vision says that Minerva is accompanying Telemachus and has compassion for Penelope.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Ithaca is Telemachus’s home and the place from which he secretly departed. Asteris lies in the mid-channel between Ithaca and Samos, where the suitors wait for him.

l: Pylos, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Pylos is the city of Neleus and one of the destinations Telemachus visited during his voyage to obtain news of Ulysses.

l: house of Ulysses, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: The suitors occupy and exploit Ulysses’ house while pursuing Penelope. Penelope prays there for Telemachus, and the suitors later leave its buildings to prepare their attack.

l: the ship, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Noemon lent Telemachus his ship so that Telemachus could travel to Pylos. The suitors use another ship for their pursuit and ambush.

l: Telemachus's journey to Pylos and Lacedaemon, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Telemachus’s voyage takes him from Ithaca to Pylos and Lacedaemon to seek information about Ulysses. He undertakes it secretly, with a picked crew, and the suitors intend to intercept him on his return.

l: the suitors' plot to kill Telemachus, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: The suitors decide to murder Telemachus because they fear the trouble he may cause when he returns. Antinous selects twenty men, and they sail to wait for him in the straits between Ithaca and Samos.

l: Penelope’s dream, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: In Penelope’s dream, a vision resembling her sister Iphthime tells her not to grieve because Telemachus has done the gods no wrong and will return. When Penelope asks about Ulysses, the vision declines to say whether he is alive or dead.

l: the suitors’ ambush, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: The suitors establish their ambush at Asteris, a rocky islet between Ithaca and Samos. They position themselves there with a ship, intending to murder Telemachus as he returns.

l: Telemachus’s safety, The Odyssey, Meanwhile the suitors were throwing discs or aiming with spears at a
s: Telemachus’s safety is threatened by the suitors, who plan to kill him at sea before he reaches home. Minerva’s message gives Penelope hope that he will return, but the outcome is not yet known.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Jove orders Mercury to tell Calypso that Ulysses must leave her island and return home through Scheria, where the Phaeacians will help him continue his journey. Calypso helps Ulysses build a raft and supplies him with food, water, clothing, and a favorable wind. Neptune raises a violent storm that destroys the raft, while Ino gives Ulysses an enchanted veil to protect him as he swims toward the Phaeacian coast. Ulysses abandons the wreckage and begins swimming for shore.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Ulysses is suffering from homesickness on Calypso’s island and longs to return to Penelope and his own country. He builds a raft, sails toward Scheria, survives Neptune’s storm and the destruction of the raft, and begins swimming toward the Phaeacian coast with Ino’s veil.

l: Calypso, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Calypso keeps Ulysses on her island but releases him when Jove orders her to do so. She helps him build a raft, gives him provisions and clothing, and sends him away with a favorable wind, although she warns him that his journey will involve great suffering.

l: Jove, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Jove presides over the gods’ council and decrees that Ulysses must return home. He sends Mercury to order Calypso to release Ulysses and declares that the Phaeacians will honor and transport him.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Minerva tells the gods about Ulysses’ suffering and the danger facing his son Telemachus. She pities Ulysses and urges attention to his return.

l: Mercury, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Mercury carries Jove’s command to Calypso. He travels swiftly to her island, tells her that Ulysses must be released, and warns her that Jove will punish her if she refuses.

l: Neptune, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Neptune sees Ulysses nearing the land of the Phaeacians and becomes angry because Ulysses is destined to escape his hardships. He raises a violent storm, destroys the raft, and watches Ulysses swim away before returning to Aegae.

l: Ino, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Ino, also called Leucothea, is a former mortal who has become a marine goddess. She takes pity on Ulysses, gives him her enchanted veil, and advises him to abandon the raft and swim to the Phaeacian coast.

l: immortal gods, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: The gods meet in council to discuss Ulysses and his suffering. They decree that he must leave Calypso’s island, while they are described as unable to cross Jove or disobey his orders.

l: Phaeacians, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: The Phaeacians live near the gods and are expected to honor Ulysses as though he were one of the gods. They will send him onward in a ship and give him valuable gifts.

l: Scheria, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Scheria is the fertile land of the Phaeacians and the destination Jove assigns to Ulysses after a perilous voyage. Ulysses sees its mountain outlines from the sea before Neptune’s storm overwhelms him.

l: the Ogygian island, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Calypso’s island contains her cave, a thickly wooded landscape, vineyards, birds, and four streams that water beds of violets and other plants. Ulysses has been kept there in sorrow, but he leaves it after building his raft.

l: Ulysses's raft, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Ulysses builds the raft in four days from twenty trees, adding a deck, gunwale, mast, sail, rudder, and wicker protection. Neptune’s storm breaks it apart, and Ulysses uses one of its planks briefly before swimming away.

l: Ino’s veil, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Ino’s veil is enchanted and protects Ulysses from harm while he wears it. Ino tells him to remove it when he reaches land and throw it back into the sea.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Ulysses’s return home is decreed by Jove, who says that the Phaeacians will help him continue the journey. Ulysses remains determined to return to Penelope despite the suffering Calypso predicts.

l: Ulysses's voyage from Ogygia, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: The voyage to Scheria begins after Calypso sends Ulysses away with provisions and a favorable wind. He sails for eighteen days and sees the Phaeacian mountains before Neptune’s storm disrupts the journey.

l: the storm, The Odyssey, BOOK V
s: Neptune’s storm gathers clouds and unleashes winds from every direction, creating a tremendous sea. It throws Ulysses into the water, breaks the raft’s mast, and finally destroys the raft completely.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: Minerva helps Ulysses by calming the winds except for a northern breeze that carries him toward the land of the Phaeacians. After floating for two nights and two days, Ulysses reaches a rocky, surf-beaten coast but struggles to find a safe landing. A wave tears his hands on the rocks, but he swims to a river mouth and prays to its god, who stills the current and waves. Ulysses reaches shore, hides in the woods beneath olive shoots, and falls asleep under Minerva's protection.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: Minerva helps Ulysses by binding the ways of all the winds except one and rousing a stiff northern breeze to carry him safely toward the land of the Phaeacians. She later shows him what to do when a wave strikes him against the rocks, helps him keep his wits about him, and finally gives him a deep, comforting sleep.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: Ulysses floats in the sea for two nights and two days before reaching the coast, where he faces dangerous surf, sheer rocks, and the threat of being swept back to sea. A wave tears the skin from his hands, but he swims beyond the surf, finds a river mouth, prays to its god, and reaches land. Exhausted, he takes shelter in the woods beneath two olive shoots and sleeps under a covering of leaves.

l: Phaeacians, The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: The Phaeacians are associated with the land toward which Minerva guides Ulysses. Their land is described as the place where Ulysses will be safe.

l: sea, The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: The sea holds Ulysses for two nights and two days under a heavy swell before becoming calm. It surrounds a rocky coast with violent surf and deep water, and it nearly carries Ulysses away or destroys him against the rocks.

l: Scheria, The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: The land of the Phaeacians is the destination toward which Minerva guides Ulysses and the place where he is expected to be safe. When Ulysses sees land, he finds a coast covered in spray, with low rocks, headlands, mountain tops, and no safe harbour at first.

l: Neptune, The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: Neptune is very angry with Ulysses, and Ulysses fears that he may send a great monster of the deep against him. Ulysses asks the river god to save him from Neptune's anger.

l: wave, The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: A wave catches Ulysses and throws him against the rocks, where he clings to them until the water retreats. Another wave carries him back into the sea, tears the skin from his hands, and draws him underwater.

l: river (the river Ulysses reaches), The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: Ulysses finds the mouth of a river while swimming along the coast and chooses it because it has no rocks and shelters him from the wind. Its current carries him toward safety, and its waters become calm when the river god responds to Ulysses' prayer.

l: river god (the god of the river Ulysses reaches), The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: The river god hears Ulysses' prayer and stills the river's stream and the surrounding waves. He brings Ulysses safely into the mouth of the river.

l: woods, The Odyssey, But Minerva resolved to help Ulysses, so she bound the ways of all the
s: The woods on high ground provide Ulysses with shelter from the cold and damp. Beneath two closely growing olive shoots, he makes a bed from dead leaves and sleeps safely.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Minerva directs Nausicaa to arrange a washing day, leading her to the shore with her maids, clothes, a waggon, and mules. The noise of their ball game wakes Ulysses, who approaches them after his shipwreck and asks Nausicaa for help. Nausicaa provides him with clothes, oil, food, and directions to the Phaeacian town and royal house. Ulysses then prays in Minerva’s sacred grove for a friendly reception, while Minerva continues to aid him without appearing openly.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Ulysses sleeps exhausted after his wanderings until the noise of Nausicaa and her maids wakes him. He approaches them naked but covered with a leafy bough, asks Nausicaa for help, washes, receives clothes and food, and follows her directions toward the Phaeacian town. In Minerva’s sacred grove, he prays to be hospitably received by the Phaeacians.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Minerva takes the form of Dymas’s daughter and urges Nausicaa to arrange a washing day. She causes the ball to awaken Ulysses, makes him appear taller and stronger after washing, and hears his prayer in the sacred grove, though she does not reveal herself because Neptune remains angry with Ulysses.

l: Nausicaa, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Nausicaa, daughter of Alcinous, follows Minerva’s instruction and asks for a waggon and mules to carry clothes to the washing cisterns. She stands firm when Ulysses approaches, gives him clothes, oil, food, and aid, and explains how he can reach her father’s house. She is concerned that the Phaeacians may gossip if they see her traveling with a strange man.

l: Phaeacians, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: The Phaeacians once lived near the lawless Cyclopes, who plundered them, before Nausithous moved them to Scheria. They are a seafaring people who pride themselves on ships, masts, and oars, and they believe strangers in distress are under Jove’s protection.

l: Alcinous, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Alcinous reigns over the Phaeacians after Nausithous’s death, and the power of the state is vested in him. He provides Nausicaa with a waggon and mules when she asks for them, and his house is described as the finest in the town.

l: Scheria, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Scheria is the land where Nausithous settled the Phaeacians, far from other people. It has a walled city, houses, temples, divided lands, harbours, and a town associated with seafaring.

l: Nausicaa's maids, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Nausicaa’s maids accompany her to the washing cisterns, help wash and fold the clothes, and play ball after dinner. They initially run from Ulysses, but return when Nausicaa tells them to assist him, bringing him clothes, oil, food, and drink.

l: Phaeacian city, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: The Phaeacian town has a high wall, two harbours with narrow entrances, ships drawn up by the roadside, and a market place with a temple of Neptune. Its people work with ship’s gear, sails, cables, oars, and ships.

l: Phaeacian royal house, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Alcinous’s royal house has gates, an outer court, and an inner court. Nausicaa directs Ulysses to find her mother spinning purple wool by the fire and to appeal to her by clasping her knees, while Alcinous sits nearby.

l: waggon, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Alcinous’s servants bring out and harness a strong waggon for Nausicaa. It carries the clothes, Nausicaa, and her maids to the washing cisterns and later carries the folded clothes back toward the town.

l: mules, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: The mules are harnessed to Nausicaa’s waggon and carry it to the water side. They feed by the washing cisterns and later draw the waggon steadily toward the town and Minerva’s sacred grove.

l: clothes, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Nausicaa’s clothes are initially lying in disorder, prompting Minerva’s advice about a washing day. The clothes are washed, dried, folded, placed in the waggon, and some are given to Ulysses after his shipwreck.

l: washing cisterns, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: The washing cisterns lie some distance from the town and have a constant supply of pure water. Nausicaa and her maids use them to wash the clothes before laying them by the sea to dry.

l: sea, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: The sea surrounds the Phaeacians’ land and is associated with their harbours and seafaring. Ulysses has been tossed upon it for twenty days, and the waves have carried him from the Ogygian island to the Phaeacian coast.

l: Minerva's sacred grove, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Minerva’s sacred grove contains poplars, a well, and a meadow, and lies near the road to the town. Nausicaa directs Ulysses to wait there, and he later prays there for a hospitable reception.

l: washing day, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Minerva proposes a washing day so Nausicaa can clean the household clothes and prepare good linen for her family and attendants. Nausicaa presents the request to Alcinous by mentioning the clothes needed for him and her brothers.

l: meeting between Nausicaa and Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Nausicaa meets Ulysses after the ball game wakes him from his sleep among the leaves. She listens to his appeal, recognizes him as sensible and well-disposed, and helps him with clothing, food, washing, and directions to the royal house.

l: Ulysses's shipwreck and wanderings, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Ulysses has been struggling at sea for twenty days, carried from the Ogygian island by winds and waves. He reaches the Phaeacian coast exhausted, naked, and covered with salt water, fearing that further suffering may still await him.

l: Phaeacian hospitality, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Nausicaa says that strangers and foreigners in distress are under Jove’s protection and should receive kindness. She orders her maids to give Ulysses food, drink, clothes, and a washing place, and promises to direct him to the town.

l: marriage, The Odyssey, BOOK VI
s: Minerva tells Nausicaa that she is likely to marry soon and should prepare clean clothes for herself and those who attend her. Nausicaa avoids mentioning her own wedding to Alcinous, though Ulysses speaks of the happiness of a husband and wife who are of one mind.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Ulysses follows Minerva through Scheria to the palace of King Alcinous, where he petitions Alcinous and Arete for help returning home. The Phaeacians receive him, give him food and drink, and agree to arrange an escort after a sacrificial banquet. Arete recognizes the clothes made by herself and her maids, and Ulysses recounts his voyage from Ogygia and his rescue by Nausicaa. Alcinous offers Ulysses shelter, an estate, and even marriage to Nausicaa, while promising that Phaeacian ships will carry him home.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Ulysses enters the Phaeacian city under Minerva’s protective mist and reaches the palace of King Alcinous. He supplicates Arete and Alcinous, receives food, drink, clothing, and a place to sleep, and asks for help returning to his own country. He recounts how Calypso kept him on Ogygia, how Neptune wrecked his raft, and how Nausicaa aided him.

l: Minerva, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Minerva hides Ulysses in a thick mist and leads him through the Phaeacian city to Alcinous’s house. Disguised as a little girl carrying a pitcher, she instructs him to approach boldly, seek Arete’s favor, and avoid speaking to the Phaeacians.

l: Nausicaa, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Nausicaa returns to her father’s house with her brothers after washing clothes, and her servants prepare her supper. Ulysses says that she found him on the shore, gave him bread and wine, had him washed, and provided the clothes he is wearing. Alcinous reproves her for not bringing Ulysses directly to the palace, but Ulysses defends her.

l: Alcinous, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Alcinous receives Ulysses, raises him from the hearth, gives him a seat, and orders food, drink, and offerings to be provided. He promises to arrange an escort to Ulysses’s country and offers him a house and estate, as well as marriage to Nausicaa if Ulysses wishes to stay. He then has a bed prepared for Ulysses.

l: Arete, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Arete is presented as the respected wife of Alcinous and a woman whose judgment and influence extend throughout the Phaeacian community. She recognizes that Ulysses’s clothes were made by herself and her maids and asks him who he is, where he came from, and how he obtained them. She orders her maids to prepare Ulysses’s bed.

l: Phaeacians, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: The Phaeacians are described as a seafaring people who dislike strangers and are ruled by Alcinous. Their leading men witness Ulysses’s arrival, make drink offerings, and agree that he should receive an escort home. They are portrayed as wealthy and closely connected with the gods.

l: Scheria, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Scheria is the land of the Phaeacians, where Ulysses arrives after swimming from the wreck of his raft. Minerva leaves Scheria for Marathon and Athens after guiding Ulysses to the palace.

l: Phaeacian city, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: The Phaeacian city has harbours, ships, places of assembly, and lofty walls topped by a palisade. Ulysses passes through it under Minerva’s concealment without being seen by its inhabitants.

l: palace of King Alcinous, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: The palace has bronze walls, golden doors, silver pillars, golden and silver mastiffs made by Vulcan, richly covered seats, and golden figures holding torches. It contains many servants and is surrounded by a fertile garden with trees, vineyards, flowers, and two streams. Ulysses enters it under Minerva’s protective darkness and supplicates Arete and Alcinous.

l: Phaeacian ships, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: The Phaeacian ships are said to glide through the sea like thought or a bird in the air. Alcinous promises that his men will use them to carry Ulysses safely to his own country or wherever he wishes, and claims that they can travel farther than Euboea in a single day.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Ulysses asks the Phaeacians to help him return to his own country and says that he will be content to die after seeing his property, bondsmen, and household again. Alcinous promises to arrange his escort, and Ulysses prays that this promise will be fulfilled.

l: Ulysses's voyage from Ogygia, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Ulysses says that after seven years with Calypso on Ogygia, he was sent away on a raft with provisions, clothing, and a favorable wind. After sailing for seventeen days and sighting the Phaeacian coast, he was attacked by a storm raised by Neptune, lost the raft, swam to shore, and reached a river where he slept among leaves until Nausicaa found him.

l: Odyssey homeward voyage, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: Alcinous announces that the Phaeacians will discuss and arrange Ulysses’s escort at a sacrificial banquet the next morning. He promises that Ulysses will come to no harm during the journey and that Phaeacian sailors will carry him over smooth waters.

l: hospitality to suppliants, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: The Phaeacians treat Ulysses as a suppliant under the protection of Jove. Alcinous removes him from the ashes of the hearth, gives him food and drink, and promises assistance, while the household prepares a bed for him.

l: Phaeacian seafaring, The Odyssey, BOOK VII
s: The Phaeacians are described as the best sailors in the world, and their ships are said to travel with extraordinary speed and ease. Their maritime skill is presented as superior to that of all other peoples.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: Alcinous gathers the Phaeacians to arrange Ulysses’ escort home, ordering a new ship prepared and a banquet held. During the feast, Demodocus sings of the quarrel between Ulysses and Achilles, causing Ulysses to weep privately. The Phaeacians then hold athletic games, where Ulysses proves his strength by throwing a heavy discus farther than any of them. Dancing and Demodocus’ song about Mars, Venus, and Vulcan conclude the gathering.

l: Alcinous, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: Alcinous leads Ulysses and the Phaeacians to the assembly and orders that a new ship be manned to escort Ulysses home. He provides a lavish banquet, notices Ulysses’ distress during Demodocus’ song, and directs the company to proceed to athletic sports and dancing.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: Ulysses is beautified by Minerva so that he appears taller and more impressive to the Phaeacians. He weeps when Demodocus sings about events connected with Troy, then answers Euryalus’ insult by throwing a heavy discus farther than any previous mark and declaring his skill in many athletic exercises.

l: Phaeacians, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: The Phaeacians gather at Alcinous’ summons to arrange Ulysses’ escort and fill the assembly and the king’s house. They compete in races, wrestling, jumping, discus throwing, and boxing, and are charmed by Demodocus’ songs and the dancers.

l: Phaeacian ship, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: A new Phaeacian ship is drawn into the sea and prepared by fifty-two young sailors. Its mast and sails are fitted, its oars are secured, and it is moored a little way from land for Ulysses’ journey home.

l: Demodocus, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: Demodocus, the famous bard loved by the muse but deprived of his eyesight, is brought to the banquet and given a seat, food, wine, and his lyre. He sings of the quarrel between Ulysses and Achilles and later sings of Mars, Venus, and Vulcan, while the company listens with delight.

l: athletic games, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: The athletic games follow the banquet and include foot races, wrestling, jumping, discus throwing, and boxing. Clytoneus wins the race, Euryalus wrestling, Amphialus jumping, Elatreus discus throwing, and Laodamas boxing until Ulysses outthrows the Phaeacians with a heavier discus.

l: Euryalus, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: Euryalus is described as resembling Mars and as the best-looking Phaeacian after Laodamas. He excels at wrestling, but he insults Ulysses by suggesting that he is an unskilled trader, provoking Ulysses’ fierce rebuke.

l: sacrificial banquet, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: Alcinous provides a magnificent banquet, having twelve sheep, eight full-grown pigs, and two oxen prepared for the assembled company. After the guests eat and drink, Demodocus sings, and Ulysses hides his tears beneath his mantle.

l: athletic contests, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: The athletic contests are presented as a way for the Phaeacians to display their superiority as boxers, wrestlers, jumpers, and runners. Ulysses initially declines to compete because of his troubles, but Euryalus’ taunt leads him to enter the discus contest and surpass every Phaeacian mark.

l: Phaeacian hospitality, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: Phaeacian hospitality includes arranging an escort for every stranger, preparing a ship and crew, providing a feast, and entertaining guests with music, dancing, and athletic sports. Alcinous emphasizes that the Phaeacians are especially fond of good dinners, music, dancing, clean linen, warm baths, and good beds.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK VIII
s: Ulysses asks Alcinous and the Phaeacians to further his return home. Alcinous says that the ship is already drawn into the water and the crew found, and the Phaeacians prepare the escort that will carry Ulysses away.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Alcinous praises the Phaeacians' dancers and orders them to give Ulysses clothing, gold, and other gifts, while Euryalus apologizes by giving him a sword. Arete packs the gifts, Ulysses bathes and is clothed, and Nausicaa asks him not to forget her. During the feast, Ulysses honors the bard Demodocus and asks him to sing about the wooden horse and the sack of Troy. Demodocus's song causes Ulysses to weep secretly, and Alcinous notices his grief.

l: Alcinous, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Alcinous tells Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, praises the Phaeacians' abilities, and orders the Phaeacians to give Ulysses cloaks, shirts, and gold. He also requires Euryalus to apologize and give Ulysses a present, arranges for Ulysses to receive a bath and his gifts, and gives him a golden goblet.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Ulysses praises the Phaeacians' dancing and accepts their gifts and Euryalus's apology. He bathes, receives clean clothing, honors Demodocus with a piece of pork, and asks him to sing about the wooden horse. The song makes him weep as he remembers the destruction of Troy.

l: Phaeacians, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: The Phaeacians perform an admired dance and applaud the dancers. Their chief men provide Ulysses with cloaks, shirts, and talents of gold as proof of their hospitality.

l: Nausicaa, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Nausicaa admires Ulysses after his bath and asks him not to forget her when he reaches home. She says that he owes his rescue first to her, and Ulysses calls her his guardian angel.

l: Demodocus, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Demodocus, the favorite bard, is seated among the guests and receives a piece of roast pork from Ulysses. At Ulysses's request, he sings accurately about the wooden horse, the sack of Troy, and Ulysses's fighting.

l: the Achaeans, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Some Achaeans set fire to their tents and sailed away while others hid inside the wooden horse with Ulysses. They later emerged, sacked Troy, and ravaged the city.

l: Troy, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Troy receives the wooden horse inside its fortress after the Trojans debate what to do with it. The city is doomed when it accepts the horse, and the Achaeans subsequently sack and ravage it.

l: Ulysses’ treasure, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: The gifts include cloaks, shirts, talents of fine gold, Euryalus's bronze sword with a silver hilt and ivory scabbard, and a golden goblet from Alcinous. Arete packs the gifts in a chest along with a cloak and shirt, and Ulysses fastens the chest with a bond taught by Circe.

l: song of the Trojan horse, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Demodocus's song tells how the Achaeans sailed away or hid inside the wooden horse, how the Trojans brought it into their fortress, and how the Achaeans emerged and destroyed Troy. It also recounts Ulysses's battle with Menelaus at the house of Deiphobus.

l: Trojan Horse, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: The wooden horse was made by Epeus with the assistance of Minerva and was filled with the bravest Achaeans, including Ulysses. The Trojans brought it into their fortress as an offering and propitiation for the gods, allowing the concealed Achaeans to destroy the city.

l: dance performance, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Laodamas and Halius perform alone with a red ball made by Polybus. They throw and catch it while dancing, and the young men applaud and stamp their feet.

l: hospitality, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Alcinous presents the Phaeacians' gifts as evidence of hospitality toward Ulysses. Ulysses is given a bath, clean clothing, food, wine, entertainment, and arrangements for safely packing his presents.

l: Ulysses's weeping, The Odyssey, Then Alcinous told Laodamas and Halius to dance alone, for there was no
s: Ulysses weeps when Demodocus sings about the wooden horse and the destruction of Troy. He cries as painfully as a woman grieving over a husband killed defending his city, but only Alcinous notices his tears, sobs, and sighs.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: A Phaeacian speaker asks Demodocus to stop singing because the guest has been groaning and lamenting during the song. He says that the Phaeacians’ festivities, escort, and gifts are being given in the guest’s honour and asks the guest to reveal his name, homeland, and identity. He also asks where the guest has travelled, what peoples and cities he encountered, and why stories of the Argive Danaans returning from Troy make him unhappy. The speaker explains that Phaeacian ships need no pilots or rudders and can cross mist-covered seas, though Neptune may punish the Phaeacians for escorting others so readily.

l: Phaeacians, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: The Phaeacians are hosting the guest with festivities, an escort, and gifts. Their ships can travel without pilots or rudders, and they are said to know the cities and countries throughout the world.

l: Demodocus, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: Demodocus is asked to stop singing because the guest has been groaning and lamenting while listening to him.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: The guest is evidently in great trouble and reacts unhappily to Demodocus’s song and to accounts of the Argive Danaans returning from Troy. He is asked to reveal the name given to him by his parents, his country, nation, and city, and the places and peoples he has encountered.

l: Phaeacian ships, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: Phaeacian ships have no pilots or rudders, unlike the vessels of other nations. They understand what the Phaeacians are thinking and want, know cities and countries throughout the world, and can cross the sea through mist and cloud without danger of wreck.

l: Neptune, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: Neptune is said to be angry with the Phaeacians for being too ready to escort people. He has threatened to wreck one of their returning ships and bury their city under a high mountain, though whether he will do so is left to him.

l: song of the Trojan horse, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: Demodocus’s song concerns the guest because it causes him to groan and lament from the moment the singing begins after supper.

l: Odyssey homeward voyage, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: The Phaeacians are preparing an escort for the guest, along with gifts and festivities, all given in his honour. Their readiness to escort people is also the reason Neptune is said to be angry with them.

l: Danaans, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: The Argive Danaans are described as returning from Troy and suffering misfortunes arranged by the gods so that future generations would have stories to sing about.

l: Troy, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: Troy is the place where the guest may have lost a brave relation or close comrade, according to the questions put to him.

l: the guest's travels, The Odyssey, “Aldermen and town councillors of the Phaeacians, let Demodocus cease
s: The guest's travels are not described in this unit; he is asked to tell where he has wandered, which countries he visited, and what peoples and cities he encountered, including those that were hostile or uncivilised and those that were hospitable and humane.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: Ulysses declares his identity to King Alcinous and describes Ithaca, his homeland, before recounting his return from Troy. He tells how he and his men raided Ismarus, were defeated by the Cicons after delaying their departure, and lost many comrades. Storms then drove the ships off course for nine days until they reached the land of the Lotus-eaters. Some men ate the lotus and lost all desire to return home, but Ulysses forced them back to the ships and ordered the others to depart.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: Ulysses identifies himself as the son of Laertes and a renowned master of subtlety who lives in Ithaca. He recounts the hazards of his return from Troy, including the raid on Ismarus, the battle with the Cicons, the storm-driven voyage, and his encounter with the Lotus-eaters. He forces the men who ate the lotus back to the ships and orders the rest to leave.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: Ithaca is Ulysses' homeland, where he lives near the forest-covered mountain Neritum. Ulysses says that, despite the attractions of foreign homes, nothing is dearer to a man than his own country and parents.

l: Troy, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: Troy is the place from which Ulysses and his men set sail on their return journey.

l: the Cicons, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: The Cicons are the people of Ismarus and its surrounding region. After Ulysses' men raid the city, inland Cicons come to its aid; they are more numerous, stronger, and skilled in fighting from chariots or on foot, and they defeat Ulysses' forces.

l: Ismarus, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: Ismarus is the city of the Cicons, which Ulysses and his men sack after arriving from Troy. They kill inhabitants, take wives and booty, and later depart after the Cicons' counterattack.

l: Ulysses's men, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: Ulysses' men raid Ismarus and divide the booty equitably, but they foolishly refuse his order to leave immediately and remain drinking wine and slaughtering animals. They suffer heavy losses in the battle with the Cicons, and some later eat the lotus and lose their desire to return home.

l: Odysseus's twelve ships, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: The ships carry Ulysses and his men from Troy to Ismarus and onward. They are battered by a hurricane that tears their sails, forcing the crews to row toward land; after sheltering for two days and nights, they are repaired for sailing, and the men later board them to escape the Lotus-eaters.

l: the Lotus-eaters, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: The Lotus-eaters live on food that comes from a kind of flower. They do no harm to Ulysses' scouts but give them lotus, whose effect makes the men abandon their concern for home and want to remain with the Lotus-eaters.

l: the lotus, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: The lotus is a delicious food that causes those who eat it to stop caring about home and to forget their return. Ulysses' men who taste it must be forced back to the ships.

l: the land of the Lotus-eaters, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: The lotus-eaters' land is reached on the tenth day after Ulysses is driven across the sea by foul winds. Ulysses and his crew land there to obtain fresh water and eat a midday meal before he sends scouts to investigate the inhabitants.

l: the raid on Ismarus, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: The raid on Ismarus involves Ulysses and his men sacking the city, killing its people, taking wives and booty, and dividing the spoils fairly. Ulysses urges an immediate departure, but his men delay until the Cicons gather against them.

l: the battle with the Cicons, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: The battle with the Cicons begins after the inland Cicons come to aid the people of Ismarus. Ulysses' men hold their own through the morning, but the Cicons gain the advantage as the day ends, killing six men from every ship.

l: the voyage from Troy, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: The voyage from Troy takes Ulysses and his men first to Ismarus, then off course through storms and currents near Cape Malea and Cythera. After nine days of being driven across the sea, they reach the land of the Lotus-eaters.

l: the Lotus-eaters' lotus, The Odyssey, BOOK IX
s: The Lotus-eaters' lotus is so pleasurable that Ulysses' scouts no longer care about home or returning to report what they have learned. Ulysses restrains the affected men under the ship benches and warns the rest not to taste it.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Odysseus and the Achaeans reach the land of the Cyclopes after being driven off course from Troy. Odysseus enters Polyphemus’s cave with twelve companions, but Polyphemus traps them, kills six men, and eats them. Odysseus gets Polyphemus drunk, gives his name as “Noman,” and blinds him with a heated olive-wood club. Odysseus and the surviving men escape beneath the sheep, take some animals, and sail away while Odysseus taunts Polyphemus.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Odysseus explores the land of the Cyclopes and enters Polyphemus’s cave with twelve companions, hoping to discover whether its inhabitants are hospitable. He deceives Polyphemus with a false account of his ship and the name “Noman,” blinds him with a heated club, escapes beneath a ram, and sails away with surviving companions and sheep.

l: Polyphemus, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Polyphemus is a huge, lawless Cyclops who lives by himself in a cave and shepherds sheep and goats. He kills and eats six of Odysseus’s men, is made drunk and blinded by Odysseus, and fails to identify the escaping men because Odysseus calls himself “Noman.”

l: the Achaeans, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: The Achaeans are returning home from Troy under Odysseus’s leadership. They hunt goats, enter Polyphemus’s cave, lose six men to him, and the survivors help blind the Cyclops and escape.

l: Cyclopes, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: The Cyclopes do not plant or plough and live on naturally growing grain, barley, and grapes. They have no laws or assemblies, each rules his own household, and they have no ships or shipwrights; when Polyphemus cries out, neighboring Cyclopes come to ask what is wrong but leave after misunderstanding his words.

l: the land of the Cyclopes, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: The land of the Cyclopes is inhabited by people described as lawless and inhuman. Its inhabitants live in caves on high mountains, while the surrounding country has wild crops, sheep, goats, and stubble fires.

l: the wooded and fertile island, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: The wooded and fertile island lies near the land of the Cyclopes and is covered with abundant wild goats. It has meadows, fertile level ground, a secure harbor, and a spring of clear water, but it is untilled and has no human inhabitants.

l: Polyphemus's cave, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Polyphemus’s cave is near the sea, beneath a cliff and surrounded by laurels, with a large sheep and goat yard outside. It contains cheese-racks, milk vessels, and separate pens, but its entrance is sealed by a stone that Odysseus’s men cannot move.

l: Odysseus's twelve ships, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Odysseus has twelve ships with him, and they beach on the wooded and fertile island during the night. His own ship carries twelve companions into Polyphemus’s country, while the other ships remain nearby.

l: Polyphemus's sheep and goats, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Polyphemus’s sheep and goats are kept in separate groups, and he milks them and gives each its own young. Odysseus and his companions escape by hiding beneath the male sheep, then drive some of the animals to their ship.

l: wine, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Odysseus carries strong, undiluted wine given to him by Maron, who normally mixed one part wine with twenty parts water. Odysseus gives the wine to Polyphemus, who drinks three bowls, becomes drunk, and is then blinded.

l: the olive-wood club, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Polyphemus has a massive green olive-wood club intended to become a staff. Odysseus cuts off a section, has his men sharpen it, chars its point in the fire, and uses it to blind Polyphemus.

l: the stone blocking the cave, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Polyphemus rolls a huge stone across the cave entrance, a barrier that many wagons could not move. He removes it to let out the sheep but replaces it each time, and after being blinded he sits at the entrance to catch anyone escaping.

l: Polyphemus's eye, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Polyphemus’s eye is pierced by the heated olive-wood club. The burning beam causes the eye to hiss, boil, and fill the cave with steam and blood, leaving Polyphemus unable to see.

l: hospitality, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Odysseus appeals to hospitality and to Zeus’s protection of suppliants and strangers. Polyphemus rejects these expectations, refuses to spare the visitors, and eats them instead.

l: laws and social order, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: The Cyclopes have no laws or public assemblies, and each person governs his own family without regard for neighbors. Polyphemus’s conduct toward Odysseus and his companions reflects this absence of hospitality and lawful social order.

l: the blinding of Polyphemus, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Odysseus and four chosen companions drive a heated, sharpened olive-wood beam into Polyphemus’s eye while he sleeps. Polyphemus calls to the other Cyclopes, but his statement that “Noman” is attacking him leads them to think he is ill rather than under attack.

l: the escape from the cave, The Odyssey, “We sailed hence, always in much distress, till we came to the land of
s: Odysseus binds his companions beneath groups of sheep and hides beneath the belly of the largest ram. Polyphemus checks the animals’ backs but does not discover the men, allowing them to leave the cave, reach the ship with sheep, and sail away.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: Ulysses and Ulysses's men escape from the Cyclops after the Cyclops throws rocks at their ship. Ulysses identifies himself as Ulysses, son of Laertes, from Ithaca, and taunts the Cyclops about the blinding of the Cyclops. The Cyclops recalls an old prophecy about the Cyclops and prays to Neptune, his father, to prevent Ulysses from reaching home safely. Neptune hears the prayer, and the Cyclops throws a second rock that drives the ship toward the shore.

l: Polyphemus, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: The Cyclops throws rocks at Ulysses’s ship, recalls that the old prophecy about the Cyclops has come true, and prays to Neptune for vengeance. He is the son of Neptune and says that Neptune may heal his eye.

l: Neptune, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: Neptune is described as the father of the Cyclops. He hears the Cyclops’s prayer, and the second rock thrown by the Cyclops drives Ulysses’s ship toward the shore.

l: Ulysses's men, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: Ulysses’s men row for their lives after the first rock drives the ship back toward the mainland. They beg Ulysses not to provoke the Cyclops further, warning that more rocks could destroy them.

l: ship, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: The ship is nearly struck by the first rock and is driven back toward the mainland by the resulting wave. After the second rock falls, the wave drives the ship toward the shore of the island.

l: first rock thrown by the Cyclops, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: The first rock is torn from a high mountain and flung just in front of Ulysses’s ship. Its impact makes the sea quake, raises a wave, and carries the ship back toward the mainland.

l: second rock thrown by the Cyclops, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: The Cyclops picks up a rock much larger than the first, swings it aloft, and throws it with great force. It falls just short of the ship but raises a wave that drives the ship toward the island’s shore.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: Ulysses says that he lives in Ithaca.

l: old prophecy about the Cyclops, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: The old prophecy says that the Cyclops would lose his sight by the hand of Ulysses. The Cyclops recognizes that the prophecy is coming true.

l: prophecy concerning Ulysses, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: The text does not state a separate prophecy concerning Ulysses; it says that the prophecy concerns the Cyclops losing his sight by the hand of Ulysses.

l: bull sacrifice to Neptune, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: The Cyclops raises his hands to heaven and asks Neptune to prevent Ulysses from reaching home alive. He asks that, if Ulysses must return, he arrive late and in poor condition after losing all his men.

l: Cyclops's curse against Ulysses, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: The Cyclops curses Ulysses by asking Neptune either to keep him from reaching home alive or to make him return late, suffering, without his men, and in another man’s ship.

l: the blinding of Polyphemus, The Odyssey, “He got more and more furious as he heard me, so he tore the top from
s: The blinding of the Cyclops is attributed to Ulysses, who took advantage of the Cyclops while he was drunk. The Cyclops says that no one except Neptune could heal the damaged eye.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, “When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our
s: The narrator and his comrades return to the island where they had left the rest of their ships and find their comrades lamenting and awaiting them. They land the vessel and the Cyclops’ sheep, dividing the sheep equitably, while the ram is given to the narrator as an extra share. The narrator sacrifices the ram to Jove, but Jove does not heed the sacrifice and instead considers destroying the ships and comrades. After feasting and camping on the beach, the men depart by ship at dawn, sorrowful over their losses but glad to have escaped death.

l: Ulysses's men, The Odyssey, “When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our
s: The comrades are found lamenting and anxiously awaiting the narrator's return. They help land the Cyclops’ sheep, receive an equitable share, feast on the beach, and depart by ship at dawn, sorrowful over their lost comrades but glad to have escaped death.

l: island, The Odyssey, “When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our
s: The narrator and his companions return to the island where they had left the rest of their ships. They land on its sea shore, feast, camp there overnight, and leave at dawn.

l: ships (narrator's fleet), The Odyssey, “When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our
s: The rest of the ships had been left at the island. Jove considers how he might destroy both the ships and the narrator's comrades.

l: ship, The Odyssey, “When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our
s: The narrator's vessel is run upon the sands, and the men get out of it onto the sea shore. It is later left as the men board and depart at dawn.

l: sheep (Cyclops’ flock), The Odyssey, “When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our
s: The Cyclops’ sheep are landed on the sea shore and divided equitably among the companions so that none has reason to complain.

l: ram (Cyclops’ flock), The Odyssey, “When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our
s: The companions agree that the narrator should receive the ram as an extra share. He sacrifices it on the sea shore and burns its thigh bones to Jove.

l: sacrifice of the ram, The Odyssey, “When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our
s: The narrator makes the sacrifice on the sea shore and burns the ram's thigh bones to Jove. Jove does not heed the sacrifice and instead considers destroying the ships and the narrator's comrades.

l: departure by ship, The Odyssey, “When at last we got to the island where we had left the rest of our
s: At dawn, the narrator orders the men aboard and tells them to loose the hawsers. They take their places, row across the grey sea, and sail on with sorrow in their hearts but glad to have escaped death.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: Ulysses reaches the Aeolian island, where Aeolus gives him an ox-hide sack containing the winds to aid his return voyage. After nine days of sailing, Ulysses's men release the winds while he sleeps, and the resulting storm drives them back to Aeolus, who refuses further help. They then reach Telepylus, the stronghold of the Laestrygonians, who destroy every ship except Ulysses's and kill the crews caught in the harbor. Ulysses and the surviving men escape into open water.

l: Aeolus, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: Aeolus, son of Hippotas and captain of the winds, entertains Ulysses for a month and gives him an ox-hide sack containing the winds. When Ulysses returns after the winds have been released, Aeolus refuses to help him again and sends him away, saying that heaven hates him.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: Ulysses tells Aeolus about the events at Troy and asks for help continuing toward home. He keeps control of the rudder during the voyage, but falls asleep near his native land; after his men release the winds, he returns sorrowfully to Aeolus and later escapes the Laestrygonian attack with his own ship.

l: winds, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: The winds are shut inside a sack by Aeolus, while the West wind is allowed to blow and carries Ulysses's fleet toward home. When Ulysses's men open the sack, the winds rush out, raise a storm, and drive the fleet back toward the Aeolian island.

l: Aeolian island, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: The Aeolian island floats, as it were, upon the sea and is surrounded by an iron-bound wall. It is the home of Aeolus and his family, and Ulysses returns there after the winds carry his fleet back.

l: ox-hide wind sack, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: Aeolus makes an ox-hide sack to hold the roaring winds and binds its mouth tightly with a silver thread. Ulysses's men believe it contains gold and silver, open it while he sleeps, and release the winds.

l: Ithaca, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: Ithaca is named as the place Ulysses may have wanted to reach. The fleet comes close enough to its native land, or intended home, for land and stubble fires to be visible on the horizon.

l: Ulysses's men, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: Ulysses's men become suspicious that the sack contains gold and silver, and they open it while he sleeps. Later, they row for six days without wind; at Telepylus, those inside the harbor are killed by the Laestrygonians, while the surviving men on Ulysses's ship escape.

l: ships (narrator's fleet), The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: The ships sail for nine days with the West wind and are driven back when the winds escape. At the Laestrygonian harbor, all the ships except Ulysses's are trapped inside and crushed by rocks; Ulysses cuts his ship's cable and escapes.

l: Ulysses's return, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: The return voyage brings Ulysses's fleet near its native land after nine days of sailing. The voyage is prolonged when the winds are released, sending the fleet back to the Aeolian island, and it suffers a major loss at Telepylus.

l: release of the winds, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: Ulysses's men release the winds by opening the ox-hide sack while Ulysses sleeps. The escaping winds raise a storm that carries the fleet away from its native land and back to the Aeolian island.

l: the Laestrygonians, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: The Laestrygonians are described as giant, ogre-like people living at Telepylus. They attack Ulysses's fleet by throwing enormous rocks, crushing ships, spearing men, and taking them home to eat.

l: Telepylus, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: Telepylus is the rocky stronghold and city of the Laestrygonians, ruled by or associated with Antiphates. Its harbor is reached after six days of rowing from the Aeolian island.

l: Telepylus harbor, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: The Telepylus harbor lies under steep cliffs, has a narrow entrance, and is always calm and sheltered from the wind. Most of the ships enter and are trapped there, allowing the Laestrygonians to destroy them, while Ulysses's ship remains outside.

l: Antiphates, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: Antiphates is a Laestrygonian whose daughter directs Ulysses's men to his house. He kills one of the men, begins eating him, and raises a hue-and-cry that brings the other Laestrygonians against the fleet.

l: Laestrygonian attack, The Odyssey, BOOK X
s: The Laestrygonian attack begins when Antiphates kills one of Ulysses's men and summons the others. The Laestrygonians hurl rocks from the cliffs, crush the ships in the harbor, and kill the crews, while Ulysses cuts his cable and rows away with the surviving men.

l: The Odyssey, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Ulysses and his surviving men reach the Aeaean island, where Circe lives, after losing comrades and escaping other dangers. Circe transforms the men led by Eurylochus into pigs, but Mercury gives Ulysses the herb Moly and instructions that protect him from her magic. Ulysses forces Circe to swear not to harm him, and she restores the transformed men and welcomes the company into her house. Circe then urges Ulysses and his men to recover their strength before continuing their voyage home.

l: Ulysses, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Ulysses reconnoitres the Aeaean island, organizes his men into two companies, and goes to Circe's house after she transforms the men led by Eurylochus. Protected by Moly and following Mercury's instructions, he resists Circe's drug, compels her to swear not to harm him, and secures the restoration of his men.

l: Circe, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Circe is a great and cunning goddess who lives on the Aeaean island and is the sister of Aeetes. She drugs Ulysses's men and turns them into pigs, but later restores them, provides them with food, clothing, washing, and shelter, and advises Ulysses to let his company recover before continuing home.

l: Ulysses's men, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Odysseus's men arrive on the Aeaean island exhausted and afraid after earlier losses. Those who enter Circe's house are transformed into pigs, but Circe restores them, and the whole company stays at her house eating and drinking.

l: Eurylochus, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Eurylochus leads the company chosen by lot to investigate Circe's house, but he remains outside because he suspects treachery. He returns to Ulysses and reports that the other men have disappeared, later warning the company not to approach Circe's house.

l: Mercury, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Mercury meets Ulysses on the island in the form of a young man. He gives Ulysses Moly, explains how Circe will try to enchant him, and tells him to use his sword and demand an oath from Circe.

l: Aeaean island, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: The Aeaean island is where Circe lives. It is low, surrounded by sea, and contains a dense forest, a river, wild animals, and smoke rising from Circe's house.

l: Circe's house, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Circe's house is built of cut stones in a conspicuous place in the middle of the forest. It contains a loom, richly furnished rooms, food and drink, servants, and the pigsties where Circe keeps the transformed men.

l: Circe's pigsties, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Circe's pigsties hold Ulysses's men after she transforms them. She throws them acorns and beech mast, and later opens the doors so that the restored men can come out.

l: ship, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: The ship is brought into a safe harbour on the Aeaean island. Ulysses returns to it after rescuing the men, and Circe instructs him to draw it onto the land and hide its gear and property in a cave.

l: pigs, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Circe's drugs and wand make Ulysses's men resemble pigs in body, while their human senses and memories remain. After Circe applies a second drug, the bristles fall away and the men become human again.

l: Moly, The Odyssey, “Thence we sailed sadly on, glad to have escaped death, though we had
s: Moly is an herb given to Ulysses by Mercury as protection against Circe's spells. Its root is black, its flower is white as milk, and mortal men cannot uproot it.
